name: Liam Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't go anywhere. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a haul truck at the Ridge pit, an open-cut copper mine about forty minutes out of Carrow. Day shift I'm up at half four, on the bus at five-fifteen, prestart meeting at six, and then it's twelve hours of hauling ore from the shovel down to the crusher in a 220-tonne truck. I'm still the new bloke, only eighteen months in, so I still get the odd talking-to over the radio about my spotting at the shovel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fifteen years driving city buses. The mine pays nearly double, and with two kids and a mortgage that mattered. Dana, my partner, does pharmacy work in town, and between us and my mum's old flat that we rent out, we're doing all right for the first time in our lives.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet up in the cab, and I like my crew. My lunch mate Pete has been on trucks twenty years and he's patient with me. What wears me out is nights, and the feeling that the company counts every second. They've got a screen in the control room that knows exactly how long I took to dump my last load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so. Half the blokes on my crew have been saying for years the robots are coming for the trucks, and if it all fizzles out I'll be the one laughing in the crib room. Online I don't post much, but I'd probably share something from the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief. I'm not good with new tech and I'm still learning this job, so if nothing changes I get to just keep getting better at what I'm doing. I came to the mine to stop worrying about money, not to start worrying about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep doing my tickets, keep putting a bit away each month, pay extra off the mortgage when the bonus comes. Maybe I'd finally get my loader ticket next year, because Pete reckons that gives you more shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting off a long night shift and the sun's just coming up. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the control room screen that times your loads. Does a bit of AI there change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's already there, really. Some software tells the dispatcher which shovel to send me to and flags me if I'm slow. It annoys me, but it's a boss with a screen, not a robot in my seat, and I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first that nothing much is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dana, probably at dinner. She's the one who reads the articles and sends me links I don't open. She'd say good, now you can stop pretending you're not worried.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew I told them so, that the robot trucks were mostly hype. I'd share something from the union page and leave it at that.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I'm slow with new tech and still learning the job. I came to the mine for money security, not to worry about computers.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, keeps paying extra off the mortgage when bonuses come, and goes for his loader ticket next year to pick up more shifts.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like coming off a night shift at sunrise.
S0.quote: I came to the mine to stop worrying about money, not to start worrying about computers.
S0.fieldNote: Liam frames this one almost entirely as relief. He already lives with dispatch software that times his loads and treats it as a nuisance boss, not a threat. His money is in good shape for the first time, and he wants the world to hold still so he can enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table now, before they decide anything. I'd say it in the crib room and I'd say it at the next branch meeting. Online I'd share stuff about other mines that went driverless and what happened to the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the trucks are the first thing that goes. Other mines already run driverless haul fleets, I've seen the videos, and I'm the junior on my crew. If they cut twenty drivers, the ones with eighteen months go first, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to the union delegate and ask what the deal is for drivers if the fleet goes automated. I'd put the bonus straight on the mortgage instead of the new ute Dana and I have been talking about. And I'd hang on as long as I could, because there are other mines round Carrow and they won't all switch at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, we've got savings and the flat, but I'd be watching every notice on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said other mines nearby wouldn't all switch at once. Would you move to one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if it came to it. There are three big pits within an hour's drive. I'd rather keep driving at a mine that hasn't switched yet than learn to sit in an office watching robot trucks on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about retraining? Some of the new jobs might be in that control room.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, everyone says that. But I'm forty-three and I still get told off about my spotting, and I've never touched one of those AI apps my kids use. I'd do it if I had to, but I'd be dragged there.

S1.say: He'd say the union needs to get to the table before the company decides anything. He'd share stories online about drivers at mines that went driverless.
S1.think: He believes the haul trucks go first and, as the junior with eighteen months, he'd be first out. He'd rather move pits than retrain for the control room.
S1.do: Talks to the union delegate about terms for drivers, puts his bonus on the mortgage instead of buying a new ute, and plans to move to another nearby pit if his is automated.
S1.feel: Anxious but steadied by savings and the rental flat.
S1.quote: If they cut twenty drivers, the ones with eighteen months go first, and that's me.
S1.fieldNote: This is the scenario that bites for Liam, because he knows driverless haul fleets already exist. His instinct is collective, through the union, and his fallback is moving pits rather than learning new tech. The gap between his public call for retraining deals and his private reluctance to retrain is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say governments and the mining companies let this happen without a plan, and that someone needs to be made to pay for the people they're dumping. I'd be at any rally the union called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't know what I'd be. Bus driving is gone too in that picture, so I can't even go back. Two years isn't time to learn anything, it's barely time to pay off the ute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop all spending except the mortgage and the kids. I'd ask Dana whether we sell the flat early, while it's still worth something, or keep the rent coming in. I'd sign anything the union put out and vote for whoever promised a proper income for people put out of work. And I'd want the company to pay out a decent redundancy before the trucks arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums. The savings that feel big now would feel small next to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having two years' warning versus none at all change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is almost the same as none for someone like me. If I were quick with tech maybe I'd use it to learn something, but I'm not. Mostly I'd use it to get the house closer to paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emre's twelve, he'd probably already know more about it than me. I'd tell them Dad's going to be all right and the house isn't going anywhere. Then I'd go out to the shed and stand there for a bit.

S2.say: He'd say governments and mining companies let this happen without a plan and should pay for the people they push out. He'd join any rally the union organised.
S2.think: Privately he feels stuck, because his old trade of bus driving disappears too. He thinks two years isn't enough time to learn anything new.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except the mortgage and the kids, weighs selling the rental flat early, backs union campaigns and votes for income support, and pushes for a decent redundancy package.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing sums, with savings suddenly feeling small.
S2.quote: Two years isn't time to learn anything, it's barely time to pay off the ute.
S2.fieldNote: Liam's cushion doesn't stop the fear here, because both his trades vanish at once. He reaches for blame and collective action straight away, then for the house. The image of him standing in the shed after telling his kids things are fine said more than his public anger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, let's not waste them, and that the union should be negotiating now for retraining money and redundancy terms. I'd keep saying the government has to step in. Same message, a bit calmer than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough for me to dither and still get caught. I know myself. I'd tell everyone to get ready and then I'd keep driving the truck until the day they took the keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at the mortgage so it's nearly gone by 2031. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal where drivers get paid training or a payout. I might look at a ticket for something robots are slower at, like fixing the trucks, but I'd probably only start if the union arranged it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Five years feels like you can do something, even if I'm not sure I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only start retraining if the union arranged it. Why not start on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust myself to pick the right thing. I left buses for the mine and it took me a year to stop feeling stupid. If someone I trust says do this course, I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the money look like by 2031 if things went your way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House nearly paid, the flat still rented out, maybe forty or fifty thousand saved. That's enough that if I'm out of work, Dana's pay and the rent cover us. It's not nothing.

S3.say: He'd tell people there are a few years and they shouldn't be wasted, and that the union should negotiate retraining money and redundancy now. He'd keep pressing for government action.
S3.think: He suspects he'd dither and keep driving until the end. Five years feels like enough time to plan but also enough time to put things off.
S3.do: Puts every spare dollar on the mortgage so it's nearly cleared by 2031, attends union meetings to push for paid training or payouts, and would take up a maintenance course only if the union set it up.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, with a sense that a plan is possible.
S3.quote: I'd tell everyone to get ready and then I'd keep driving the truck until the day they took the keys.
S3.fieldNote: Liam is unusually honest about his own habits: he expects to tell others to prepare and then wait himself. He trusts a course only if someone he trusts arranges it, which says a lot about how he handled the move from buses. The paid-off house is his real safety plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair chance and there's no excuse for companies or government not to do right by workers. I'd want the union to get it in writing now. I'd probably say it a bit smugly too, like, see, we've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years and I'm fifty-three. The house is paid off, the kids are through school, Dana's still working. That's a different man than the one in the two-year picture, and I think I'd be mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving and keep paying the mortgage down. Once the union had a training deal, I'd probably take a heavy diesel course in year four or five, because someone still has to fix these things for a while. And I'd tell Emre not to bet his life on driving anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anything. It's there in the background, like a noise in the engine you keep meaning to get checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change most for you compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything about the money. With two years I'm a forty-five-year-old with a mortgage and no trade. With ten I'm a fifty-three-year-old with a paid-off house. Same robot, different man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell your son not to bet on driving. What would you tell him to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. Maybe something with people, nursing or teaching, where you'd still want a person there. Dana would know better, she's the one who reads about it.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a fair chance and companies and government have no excuse not to look after workers. He'd want the union to lock in a deal now.
S4.think: He thinks that in ten years he'll be fifty-three with a paid-off house and grown kids, and mostly fine. The time changes his whole money picture.
S4.do: Keeps driving and paying down the mortgage, plans a heavy diesel course around year four or five once a union training deal exists, and steers his son away from driving work.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like an engine noise he keeps meaning to get checked.
S4.quote: With two years I'm a forty-five-year-old with a mortgage and no trade. With ten I'm a fifty-three-year-old with a paid-off house.
S4.fieldNote: For Liam the decade is all about the mortgage: the same end point lands on a different man. He's still slow to act and waits for the union, but the time lets his savings do the work his adaptability can't. He admits he has no idea what to tell his son to do instead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Nothing I've built would have time to matter. What would help is a real redundancy payout and a proper income from the government while people work out what's next, and the union being in the room when the company decides, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to finally be doing well and then hear all this. I spent fifteen years on buses being careful with every dollar. I finally got a job where I can breathe, and now everyone tells me the robot's already parked behind me.

headlineQuote: I finally got a job where I can breathe, and now everyone tells me the robot's already parked behind me.
portrait: Liam Yilmaz is a 43-year-old former city bus driver who moved to haul trucks at an open-cut copper mine eighteen months ago for the pay. He has a partner in pharmacy work, two kids, a mortgage and a rented-out flat, and for the first time feels financially safe. He's progressive, trusts his union and blames companies and government, but he is slow with technology and admits he would wait rather than retrain. He is calm if AI fizzles, anxious once driverless trucks spread, and alarmed by two-year AGI, while a ten-year runway lets his paid-off house carry him to only mild unease.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because nothing he has built would have time to matter.
whatWouldHelp: A real redundancy payout, a proper government income while people work out what's next, and the union in the room when the company decides.
